origin.title: Seven origins, one birthplace of Arabica

regions.name: Yirgacheffe
regions.subtitle: SOUTHERN ETHIOPIA
regions.description: World-famous for its exquisite floral aroma, often jasmine, with bright citrusy or lemony acidity and a delicate, tea-like body. Primarily washed, Yirgacheffe is one of the most sought-after coffees in the world.

regions.name: Sidamo
regions.subtitle: SOUTHERN ETHIOPIA
regions.description: Features a vibrant, complex profile with fruity and floral notes, bright acidity, and a balanced, medium body. Sidama offers both washed and natural processed beans, each with distinct character.

regions.name: Guji
regions.subtitle: SOUTHERN OROMIA
regions.description: Gaining global acclaim for its complex fruitiness — berry, stone fruit — along with floral notes, winey acidity, and deep sweetness. Often naturally processed, showcasing intense, layered flavors.

regions.name: Harrar
regions.subtitle: EASTERN ETHIOPIA
regions.description: Renowned for its complex, winey or fruity notes, often with a distinct blueberry undertone and full body. All Harar is dry-processed (natural), with medium to light acidity and typical mocha flavor with aftertaste.

regions.name: Limmu
regions.subtitle: WESTERN ETHIOPIA
regions.description: Typically wet-processed (washed), offering a clean cup with pronounced floral and spicy notes, balanced acidity, and medium body. Limu's acidity is medium to pointed with a medium to full body and distinctive winy character.

regions.name: Jimma
regions.subtitle: SOUTHWESTERN ETHIOPIA
regions.description: Known for its balanced profile, often featuring floral notes, good acidity, and a medium body. The cup is attractive with medium acidity and a good, pleasant mouth feel.

regions.name: Lekempti
regions.subtitle: WESTERN ETHIOPIA
regions.description: Grayish in color with medium to pointed acidity and good mouth feel. Fruitiness is its unique character. Lekempti coffee from the Wollega zone is prized for its distinctive fruity profile.

hero.title: From local trade to a global coffee house.
hero.body1: Birra's story begins far from any boardroom — in a small town near Galamso, in Ethiopia's West Hararghe zone. In 2010, two young entrepreneurs with over a decade of local trading experience took their first step in business by buying and selling cattle. That early trade taught them what still defines Birra today: reading a market, building trust with suppliers, and moving goods reliably from producer to buyer.
hero.body2: As their network and capital grew, they turned to the commodity closest to the region's identity and Ethiopia's global reputation — coffee — founding Birra Coffee General Trading PLC as a licensed exporter. Named for the Oromo word for spring, the season of harvest, Birra grew step by step into a diversified trading house: exporting premium Arabica to Europe, North America, the Middle East and Asia; importing construction materials, steel, vehicles and machinery; roasting and serving coffee through its own café; and developing commercial real estate including Birra Mall in Dire Dawa and Birra Tower and Birra Plaza in Addis Ababa. Today, with processing facilities in Dire Dawa and Addis Ababa, Birra remains rooted in the same instincts that built it: start small, earn trust, and grow with integrity.

article.title: Ethiopian Coffee: From Highland Origins to Global Markets
article.dek: Discover how altitude, climate, processing and origin shape the character and value of Ethiopian coffee.

sections.title: The Birthplace of Coffee
sections.body: Coffee's story begins in Ethiopia. According to a widely told legend, a goatherd named Kaldi in the Kaffa region noticed his goats grew unusually energetic after eating the red cherries of a wild shrub — and coffee's journey into human hands began. Whatever the truth behind the story, the botany isn't in dispute: Ethiopia is the genetic home of Coffea arabica, and wild arabica trees still grow in the country's highland forests today. From here, coffee travelled north to Yemen — where the port of Mocha lent its name to the trade — and from there out into the world.

sections.title: Altitude, Climate and Soil
sections.body: Ethiopia's specialty coffee grows at elevations from roughly 1,400 up to 2,300 metres above sea level, in the cool, equatorial highlands that ring the Great Rift Valley. At altitude, cherries ripen more slowly, giving the bean more time to develop sugars and acidity — a major reason Ethiopian coffee is prized for its complexity. Volcanic, mineral-rich soil and a distinct wet and dry season add to the picture, giving each growing region its own microclimate and, in turn, its own character in the cup.
sections.quote: Altitude isn't a marketing detail — it's why a lot grown at 2,200 metres and one grown at 1,400 can taste nothing alike.

regions.title: Ethiopia's Coffee Regions
regions.body: Ethiopia's coffee is grown across a handful of distinct regions, each shaped by its own altitude, soil and microclimate. Yirgacheffe and Sidamo are known for floral, citrus-bright cups; Guji for complex, layered fruit; Harrar — one of the country's oldest coffee-growing areas, traditionally dry-processed — for its heavy body and winey, berry-like character. Further west, Limmu, Jimma and Lekempti round out a coffee geography as varied as the country itself.

processing.title: Washed, Natural and Honey
processing.body: How a cherry is processed after harvest shapes the cup as much as where it was grown. Washed processing removes the fruit before drying, producing a clean, bright cup with pronounced acidity. Natural processing dries the whole cherry around the bean, imparting a heavier body and fruit-forward, sometimes wine-like sweetness. Honey processing sits between the two — some of the fruit's mucilage is left on the bean during drying — giving a cup with more body than washed coffee and more clarity than natural.

methods.name: Washed
methods.desc: Fruit removed before drying. Clean cup, pronounced acidity.

methods.name: Natural
methods.desc: Whole cherry dried around the bean. Heavier body, fruit-forward.

methods.name: Honey
methods.desc: Partial mucilage left on during drying. Body between the two.

sections2.title: How Origin Shapes Flavor
sections2.body: Altitude, soil, varietal and processing method don't act alone — together they form what coffee people call terroir, the same idea that shapes a wine's character. A Yirgacheffe cherry grown at altitude and washed will taste nothing like a Harrar cherry dried in the sun, even though both are unmistakably Ethiopian. It's this range — one country producing cups as different as a delicate, floral Yirgacheffe and a bold, fruit-driven Harrar — that makes Ethiopian coffee unique among origins.

sections2.title: From Farm to Global Market
sections2.body: The vast majority of Ethiopian coffee is grown by smallholder farmers, many working plots of a hectare or less, often alongside other crops in the shade of native trees. Cherries are delivered to local washing or processing stations, then move through milling, grading and quality inspection before they're ready for export. Much of this coffee changes hands through the Ethiopia Commodity Exchange (ECX), which brings transparency and standardised grading to the market; the rest moves through direct relationships between exporters and producers or cooperatives.

birra.title: Birra's Role in Sourcing and Export
birra.body: Birra Coffee General Trading PLC has operated as a licensed Ethiopian coffee exporter since 2010, sourcing from seven origins — Yirgacheffe, Sidama, Guji, Harar, Limu, Jimma and Lekempti — through both the Ethiopia Commodity Exchange and direct supplier relationships. Green coffee is processed at Birra's own facilities in Dire Dawa and Sheger City, Oromia, using advanced color-sorting technology alongside experienced hand-selection, and is certified to CERES (EU-equivalent) and USDA Organic standards. From there, it ships to buyers across the Middle East, Europe, the Americas and Asia.
